title: Syncope: initial evaluation and risk stratification
subject: cardiology
summary: Confirm true syncope, then do a history, examination with lying and standing BP, and ECG; identify high-risk features suggesting cardiac syncope needing admission or urgent evaluation, and discharge low-risk reflex or orthostatic syncope with education and follow-up.

sections.title: Is it syncope?
items: Syncope: transient loss of consciousness from cerebral hypoperfusion, with rapid onset, short duration and spontaneous complete recovery.

Exclude non-syncopal causes: seizures (prolonged jerking, tongue bitten on the side, head turning, prolonged confusion), hypoglycaemia, intoxication, head injury, psychogenic pseudosyncope, and TIA (rarely causes loss of consciousness).

Classify: reflex (vasovagal, situational, carotid sinus), orthostatic hypotension (drugs, volume depletion, autonomic failure), or cardiac (arrhythmia or structural heart disease). Cardiac syncope carries the highest mortality.

sections.title: Initial evaluation (for every patient)
items: Detailed history from patient and witness: posture, trigger, prodrome, exertion, palpitations, chest pain, injury, recovery, previous episodes, medicines, family history of sudden death.
Examination including lying and standing BP (at 1 and 3 minutes), cardiac murmurs, and signs of bleeding or volume loss.
12-lead ECG for all. Capillary glucose, haemoglobin and pregnancy test where relevant; troponin, BNP or D-dimer only when the clinical picture suggests ACS, heart failure or PE.
Orthostatic hypotension: sustained fall in SBP of 20 mmHg or more, DBP 10 mmHg or more, or SBP below 90 mmHg on standing, with reproduction of symptoms.

sections.title: High-risk features (suggest cardiac syncope)
items: Event: new chest discomfort, breathlessness, abdominal pain or headache; syncope during exertion or when supine; sudden palpitations immediately followed by syncope. Minor (high risk with heart disease or abnormal ECG): no or brief prodrome, syncope while sitting, family history of sudden death at a young age.
History: severe structural or coronary heart disease (heart failure, low LVEF, previous MI).
Examination: unexplained SBP below 90 mmHg, suspected GI bleeding, persistent bradycardia below 40/min while awake and not athletic, undiagnosed systolic murmur.

ECG: acute ischaemia; Mobitz II or complete heart block; AF with slow rate below 40/min; sinus bradycardia below 40/min, sinoatrial block or pauses over 3 seconds while awake; bundle branch block or bifascicular block; Q waves or LVH suggesting cardiomyopathy; VT; pacemaker or ICD malfunction; type 1 Brugada pattern; QTc above 460 ms on repeated ECGs; pre-excitation.

Low-risk features: typical reflex prodrome (light-headedness, warmth, sweating, nausea), clear trigger (pain, fear, sight of blood, prolonged standing in a hot crowded place, cough, micturition, after a meal), syncope on standing up, similar long-standing episodes, and normal examination and ECG.

sections.title: Disposition
items: Low-risk features only: discharge from the emergency department with education and outpatient follow-up if needed.
Any high-risk feature: admit or evaluate urgently in a syncope unit or observation unit with ECG monitoring; do not discharge before cardiac causes are addressed.
Neither clearly low nor high risk: period of ED observation with ECG monitoring, or rapid access syncope clinic.
Advise on driving and hazardous work according to local regulations; driving is usually restricted after unexplained or cardiac syncope until the cause is treated.

sections.title: Further tests (guided by initial findings)
items: Echocardiography when structural heart disease is suspected. Exercise testing for syncope during or shortly after exertion.
In-hospital telemetry for high-risk patients; Holter if episodes are frequent (at least weekly); external loop recorder or implantable loop recorder for infrequent recurrent unexplained syncope.

Carotid sinus massage in patients over 40 with unexplained syncope suggestive of reflex cause (positive: asystole over 3 seconds or SBP fall over 50 mmHg with symptoms); avoid if recent TIA, stroke or carotid bruit.
Tilt testing for suspected reflex or orthostatic syncope needing confirmation; electrophysiology study in selected patients with bifascicular block or previous MI.
Do not order routine CT or MRI brain, EEG or carotid Doppler for uncomplicated syncope.

sections.title: Treatment by cause
items: Reflex syncope: explanation and reassurance, avoid triggers, adequate fluid and salt intake, physical counter-pressure manoeuvres (leg crossing, hand grip, squatting) at the onset of prodrome.

Orthostatic hypotension: stop or reduce offending drugs (diuretics, vasodilators, alpha-blockers), 2 to 3 L fluid and 10 g salt per day if not hypertensive or in heart failure, compression garments, head-up tilt sleeping; midodrine or fludrocortisone if still symptomatic.

Cardiac syncope: treat the cause (pacing for bradyarrhythmia or AV block, ablation or ICD for ventricular arrhythmia, valve intervention for severe aortic stenosis). Cardioinhibitory reflex syncope in patients over 40 with documented asystole may benefit from pacing.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Labelling exertional syncope, syncope while supine or syncope with palpitations as vasovagal.
Missing GI bleeding, ectopic pregnancy, PE, aortic dissection or aortic stenosis presenting as syncope.
Discharging an elderly patient without standing BP measurement and medication review.
Missing long QT, Brugada pattern or pre-excitation on the ECG.

drugs.name: Midodrine
drugs.dose: 2.5 to 10 mg orally three times daily (last dose at least 4 hours before bedtime)
drugs.notes: Orthostatic hypotension or refractory reflex syncope. Supine hypertension, urinary retention.

drugs.name: Fludrocortisone
drugs.notes: Orthostatic hypotension or young patients with reflex syncope and low normal BP. Hypokalaemia, supine hypertension, oedema; avoid in heart failure.
